g6-2023-014.quote: students use the order of operations to find the value of expressions with exponents
g6-2023-014.why: The item evaluates 3(7−2)+5³ over a denominator of 2, so the exponent must be resolved before the surrounding sum and division. This activity's column expressions (5+4², 2·5², 3·4²) are exactly that drill — find a numerical value where an exponent sits alongside another operation.

g6-2023-043.quote: students use the order of operations to find the value of expressions with exponents
g6-2023-043.why: The item asks for the value of 7 × (5 − 3)³ − 20 ÷ 4: parentheses, then the exponent, then multiply/divide, then subtract. The activity is the curriculum's only sustained practice at finding values of numerical expressions containing exponents.

g6-2024-014.quote: students use the order of operations to find the value of expressions with exponents
g6-2024-014.why: The item evaluates 8² ÷ 4 × 2³, which needs both exponents first and then left-to-right for the ÷ and ×. The activity drills exponent-before-multiplication (2·5², 3·4²) but nowhere rehearses a division-then-multiplication chain, which is the item's actual distractor; hence medium.

g6-2025-019.quote: Find the value of the expressions in one of the columns.
g6-2025-019.why: The item evaluates (3²+5·3)/2³, with a fraction bar acting as a grouping symbol over an exponent in the denominator. The activity is the order-of-operations-with-exponents practice, though its rows use · and + rather than a fraction bar, so the grouping-bar move is the item's own addition.

g6-2025-040.quote: students use the order of operations to find the value of expressions with exponents
g6-2025-040.why: The item evaluates 4(3 + 5²) − 6: parentheses containing an exponent, then multiply, then subtract. That is the same order-of-operations-with-exponents calculation the activity's rows require.

g6-2026-045.quote: students use the order of operations to find the value of expressions with exponents
g6-2026-045.why: The item evaluates 3(4³ − 6²) + 7(2 + 1)³ — exponents inside and outside parentheses, then multiplication and addition. The activity is where the curriculum has students find values of expressions in which exponents sit alongside other operations.

g6-2023-012.quote: Circle the expression that represents the number of inches the plant grew
g6-2023-012.why: The item asks which expression is '14 less than the product of 8 and y' (8y − 14), and its lead distractor reverses the subtraction to 14 − 8y. This Cool-down is exactly that discrimination — choose between x − 8 and 8 − x for the plant's growth — and its second question asks for a product expression, 1.2n, for n trees.

g6-2024-002.quote: Write expressions to show Clare’s age when her cousin is at different ages.
g6-2024-002.why: The item asks for '5 more than the product of 2 and y' (2y + 5). This activity is where students build such expressions from a stated relationship: 'Clare is 5 years older than her cousin' gives x + 5 and 'Diego has 3 times as many comic books as Han' gives 3n — the two moves the item combines.

g6-2025-030.quote: Circle the expression that represents the number of inches the plant grew
g6-2025-030.why: The item translates 'the sum of fifteen and five less than twice a number, n' into 15 + (2n − 5); the final discrimination between its two plausible choices is whether 'five less than twice n' is 2n − 5 or 5 − 2n. This Cool-down is the one place the curriculum tests that reversal directly. Medium because no grade 6 activity asks students to parse a nested phrase of this length from words alone; the non-Cool-down runner-up is Activity 2, 'Building Expressions' (p97).

g6-2026-030.quote: Circle the expression that represents the number of inches the plant grew
g6-2026-030.why: The item translates '55 less than the sum of 4 and twice a number, c' into (4 + 2c) − 55, and three of its four distractors turn on subtraction order or on 2(4 + c) versus 4 + 2c. The Cool-down's x − 8 versus 8 − x choice is the order discrimination; the runner-up for the expression-building half is Activity 2, 'Building Expressions' (p97).

g6-2023-018.why: The item displays 5z + (9 ÷ 3) and asks for the coefficient of the variable, with 9 and 3 from the other term as distractors. This Warm-up is the definitional moment: students meet 3 ⋅ x rewritten as 3x, and the synthesis then names 3 the coefficient. Medium because no grade 6 ACTIVITY asks a student to name a coefficient — the only 'what is the coefficient of the variable?' prompt is a practice problem in Lesson 6, 'Percentages and Equations' (p87).

g6-2025-023.quote: practice using mathematical vocabulary related to expressions, such as “coefficient,” “variable,” and “exponent.”
g6-2025-023.why: The item asks for the coefficient in 2x^3, and its distractor is 3, the exponent. This activity is the one place the curriculum makes students separate those roles — its list contrasts 3^x, 3x and 9 + x — and its narrative names 'coefficient' and 'exponent' as the vocabulary being practised. Medium: the activity has students evaluate rather than name the part.

g6-2026-038.quote: practice using mathematical vocabulary related to expressions, such as “coefficient,” “variable,” and “exponent.”
g6-2026-038.why: The item asks for the coefficient in 6n^5 as a constructed response, the same coefficient-versus-exponent separation. This activity contrasts 3^x with 3x and names 'coefficient' and 'exponent' as the vocabulary in play. Medium for the same reason: nowhere does an activity ask students to name the coefficient outright.

g6-2023-022.quote: Find the value of each expression for the given value of x
g6-2023-022.why: The item evaluates 5b + c^3 at b = 7 and c = 4 — substitute, raise to a power, multiply, add. This Cool-down is the curriculum's own test of exactly that: four expressions to evaluate at a given value, including one with the variable raised to a power and one with a coefficient (4x versus 4^x).

g6-2025-005.quote: Find the value of each expression for the given value of x
g6-2025-005.why: The item evaluates c^3 + 4h − 7 at c = 2 and h = 3, and its distractors come from mis-ordering the cube against the multiplication. The Cool-down asks for the value of expressions such as 4 + x^2 and 4x at a given value, which is the same substitute-then-order-of-operations move; the item simply carries two letters instead of one.

g6-2026-004.quote: Find the value of each expression for the given value of x
g6-2026-004.why: The item evaluates 2(12 − x) + y^2 at x = 7 and y = 3. This activity is where students evaluate expressions containing a variable with an exponent alongside a coefficient. Medium because no grade 6 activity has students substitute into a parenthesised difference like 2(12 − x); that grouping convention is settled in Lesson 14's 'Calculating Surface Area' (p185) instead.

g6-2023-035.quote: Select all the expressions that represent the large rectangle’s total area.
g6-2023-035.why: The item asks which expression is equivalent to 4(3m + 1), i.e. distribute a number over a sum containing a variable. This Cool-down is the curriculum's test of that move: students must see that 5(b + 3) and 5b + 15 are the same area, and reject 3(5 + b). Lesson 11's 'Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property' (p142) has the exact form 3(2x + 1) but that lesson is optional.

g6-2023-024.activity: Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property
g6-2023-024.why: The item needs 8(2a + 3b) − 2b rewritten as 16a + 22b: distribute over a two-term sum, then collect the b terms. This activity's table is the only place in grade 6 that asks for both moves — 3(2x + 1) for the distribution and x + 2x + 3x and 4x + 7x for the collection. The lesson is marked optional in the pacing table; the non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10's Cool-down 'Which Expressions Represent Area?' (p134), which covers the distribution but never the collecting of like terms.

g6-2026-019.activity: Writing Equivalent Expressions Using the Distributive Property
g6-2026-019.why: The item needs 5(6m + 3) + 4m rewritten as 34m + 15, and its two strongest distractors (37m, 49m) come from collecting the constant into the m term. Distribute-then-collect is asked only here, in the rows 3(2x + 1) and x + 2x + 3x. Optional lesson; non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10's Cool-down 'Which Expressions Represent Area?' (p134).

g6-2024-041.quote: Select all the expressions that represent the large rectangle’s total area.
g6-2024-041.why: The item hands students a false claim, 6 + 8x = 3(3 + 5x), and asks them to say what is wrong and to supply the real equivalent, 9 + 15x. This Cool-down is the same judgement: distribute over a sum with a variable and then decide which of five candidates — including the deliberately wrong 3(5 + b) — actually match. What the Cool-down does not require is the written critique; the definition of equivalence that the critique rests on comes from Lesson 8's 'Using Tape Diagrams to Show That Expressions Are Equivalent' (p106).

g6-2026-032.quote: Match each expression in Column A to an equivalent expression in Column B.
g6-2026-032.why: The item factors 24x + 18y into 6(4x + 3y) — pull a common factor out of a two-variable sum. This matching activity contains that exact form twice: 12a + 3b with 3(4a + b), and 6a + 10b with 2(3a + 5b). The lesson is optional in the pacing table; the non-optional runner-up is Lesson 10's 'Areas of Partitioned Rectangles' (p130), where students write each area both as a product and as a sum, but always with a diagram and never with two different variables.

g6-2024-003.quote: used in place of the variable to make the inequality true
g6-2024-003.why: The item asks which of 2, 3, 4, 5 makes 3b > 12 true. This is the activity where 'solution to an inequality' is defined as a number put in place of the variable that makes the inequality true, and where students decide whether a 55-inch rider satisfies the High Bounce requirement. Medium because every inequality in this lesson is a bare comparison (h ≥ 55); the item's 3b puts an operation on the variable, which students meet only in the equation work of Unit 6 Lesson 2, 'Find a Solution' (p38).

g6-2025-027.quote: Select all numbers that are solutions to the inequality w < 1
g6-2025-027.why: The item asks which number is NOT a solution to 3w ≥ 12, and rejecting w = 4 depends on 12 ≥ 12 being true — the boundary case. This Cool-down is the curriculum's own select-the-solutions test, and the inclusive boundary of ≥ is established in Lesson 8's 'How High and How Low Can It Be?' (p102). Medium: nothing in the Cool-down puts a coefficient on the variable.

g6-2026-026.quote: Select all numbers that are solutions to the inequality w < 1
g6-2026-026.why: The item asks which value of k makes k − 16 > 29 true, so a student must substitute, subtract and then compare. The Cool-down is where students decide which given numbers are solutions to an inequality; the subtract-then-compare half has no inequality counterpart in grade 6 and is rehearsed only on equations, in Unit 6 Lesson 2's 'Find a Solution' (p38), which includes 1,000 − a = 400.

g6-2024-022.quote: Diego has 3 times as many comic books as Han does.
g6-2024-022.why: The item says Jacob has '4 fewer than 3 times' Tammy's s stamps and asks for the expression 3s − 4. This activity is built from exactly that kind of comparison — 'Diego has 3 times as many comic books as Han' for the multiplier and 'Clare is 5 years older than her cousin' for the added or subtracted constant — with students writing the expression for an unspecified value of the variable.

g6-2026-006.activity: Partitioned Rectangles When Lengths Are Unknown
g6-2026-006.quote: Write an expression for the sum of the areas of the two rectangles.
g6-2026-006.why: The item sums six labelled sides of an L-shaped figure (2, x, 5, 2, x + 3, 6) into 2x + 18. The closest thing the curriculum asks is this activity, where students write an expression for a figure's total measurement when one length is unknown, producing a mixed expression such as 40 + 5x. Low confidence: no grade 6 activity asks for a perimeter expression at all, and collecting the figure's two x terms is rehearsed only in the optional Lesson 11, 'The Distributive Property, Part 3' (p142).

g6-2024-038.quote: Solve each equation. Explain or show your reasoning.
g6-2024-038.why: The item is a bare solve: what value of n makes n/8 = 17 true. This Cool-down is the curriculum's test of exactly that, with x + 1 3/4 = 8, 5.7x = 17.1 and a fraction-coefficient equation of the same px = q form as n · 1/8 = 17.

g6-2024-036.quote: Circle all of the equations that describe each situation. Then find the solution
g6-2024-036.why: The item gives a rate ($25.00 per hour) and a total ($62.50) and asks for the number of hours — set up 25x = 62.50 and solve. This activity is where students match a situation to a px = q equation and then solve it; its solar-panel question, 1.5p = 100, is the same shape.

g6-2025-046.quote: Circle all of the equations that describe each situation. Then find the solution
g6-2025-046.why: Both halves of the item ask students to write and solve an equation from a situation: 9 · 2x = 54 for the rug and 7p = 784 for the price. This activity is the write-and-solve home for px = q situations. Medium because the first half also needs the area of a rectangle with a side of 2x, which is set up only in Lesson 10's Warm-up 'Possible Areas' (p128).

g6-2026-027.quote: Here are three situations and six equations. Which equation best represents each situation?
g6-2026-027.why: The item asks only which equation determines the number of sugar-cookie boxes — x + 250 = 324 — and never asks students to solve it. That is precisely this activity: pick the equation that represents each story from six candidates, including the x + 5 = 20 versus 5x = 20 versus x + 20 = 5 confusions the item's distractors reproduce.

g6-2026-041.quote: Kiran scores 223 fewer points in a computer game than Mai.
g6-2026-041.why: The item says Dan has 43 fewer cards than Bella's 150 and asks students to write and solve an equation for c. This activity's first question is the same situation with different numbers — Kiran scores 223 fewer points than Mai's 409 — with students choosing among c + 43 = 150 and 150 − 43 = c forms and then finding the value.

g6-2023-040.quote: Could the area of this rectangle be 11 square units? Explain your reasoning.
g6-2023-040.why: The item composes three tiles into an x-by-5x rectangle, sets its perimeter to 60, and asks for x. This Warm-up is the nearest thing in grade 6: write a figure's measurement as an expression in a variable, then ask what value of the variable produces a stated measurement. Low confidence — no activity asks for a perimeter expression, composing figures with unknown lengths is Lesson 10's 'Partitioned Rectangles When Lengths Are Unknown' (p129), and solving 12x = 60 is Lesson 4. The item's 0.13 P-value matches how little the curriculum rehearses these steps together.

g6-2024-011.quote: closed (include) or open (exclude) circle at the boundary of the constraint
g6-2024-011.why: The item shows four number lines and asks which represents x ≥ −3; the four differ only in whether the circle at −3 is filled and which way the ray is shaded. This activity is the match between math statements and number lines, and it is where the curriculum makes the filled-versus-open circle decision explicit. The negative boundary itself is grade 6 work from this unit's Section A.

g6-2026-023.quote: Write equations and/or inequalities for the height requirements of each ride.
g6-2026-023.why: The item gives an amusement-park roller coaster with a 'must be at least 48 inches tall' requirement and asks which number line shows it. This activity is the same task in the same context — Priya's ride list includes 'Twirl-O-Coaster 58 inches minimum' — and students must both write the inequality and represent it on a number line, with the 'minimum' wording forcing the inclusive boundary the item's filled circle tests.

g6-2026-014.quote: Select all equations that can represent the relationship between b

The Cool-down tests exactly that choice between equations relating two quantities. g6-2023-046.quote: Which variable is independent variable? 2. What does the point (12, 4) represent
g6-2023-046.why: The item shows a graph of chore earnings and asks students to explain the relationship, name the dependent and independent variables, and find the earnings for 9 chores. This Cool-down asks the same three things of a distance-time graph and equation: which variable is independent, what a plotted point means in the situation, and what point would represent a value beyond the ones shown.

g6-2024-042.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs, Oh My!
g6-2024-042.quote: How the dependent variable and independent variable are related.
g6-2024-042.why: The item gives the equation c = 2.75t and asks students to describe the relationship in words and say which variable is independent and which is dependent. That is this activity's explicit deliverable — students must be prepared to explain what each variable represents and how the dependent and independent variables are related for their own assigned equation.

g6-2025-041.lessonTitle: Tables, Equations, and Graphs, Oh My!
g6-2025-041.quote: Take turns with your partner to match an equation with a table.

Medium because the card sort has students match a ready-made equation rather than write one; the write-an-equation-from-a-table task is the Cool-down of Lesson 18, 'More Relationships' (p243), which the pacing table marks optional.
